overview.summary: How strictly to govern the most capable AI systems, whether rules should target models or uses, and who holds the pen.
overview.scope_covered: Governing the most capable general-purpose models: safety mandates, transparency, liability, preemption, compute governance, global coordination.
overview.scope_excluded: Application-level AI fights with their own debates: copyright and training data, deepfakes, hiring-bias audits, autonomous weapons, AI job loss.
overview.why_now: A December 2025 US executive order pushing federal preemption of state AI laws collided with the first state frontier-safety statutes taking effect, making who writes the rules the live fight.

stats.label: AI researchers’ estimate of extinction-level risk · 2,778-researcher survey
stats.note: Median 5 percent for outcomes as bad as human extinction, rising to 10 percent for losing control of advanced AI; the same researchers were mostly optimistic overall, 68 percent expecting good outcomes.
stats.detail: From the 2023 Expert Survey on Progress in AI, fielded in October 2023 and published in January 2024 by Katja Grace and colleagues: 2,778 researchers who had published at top-tier AI venues, the largest survey of its kind. Median probabilities for extremely bad outcomes such as human extinction came in at 5 percent, rising to 10 percent when the question was phrased as human inability to control advanced AI; means ran far higher, 14 to 19 percent, pulled up by a minority of very high estimates. Between 38 and 51 percent of respondents gave at least a 10 percent chance to outcomes as bad as extinction, and the same respondents were mostly optimistic on balance: 68 percent thought good outcomes from superhuman AI more likely than bad ones. Estimates vary widely by subfield and by question wording, and many researchers reject the exercise as unfalsifiable.
stats.source_label: Grace et al., Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI

stats.label: Growth in frontier training compute · Epoch AI trend since 2020
stats.note: Frontier training compute has grown roughly fivefold a year since 2020, so a fixed threshold drifts from ‘frontier’ toward ordinary within a few years.
stats.detail: Aggregate compute deployed in top training runs has grown about 10,000-fold since 2020. Training cost has grown more slowly, roughly 3.5× a year (doubling near every 7 months), partly offset by algorithmic efficiency gains that cut the compute needed for equivalent performance by roughly two-thirds a year. Any static FLOP threshold written into law (EU AI Act, California SB 53) keeps capturing a different, growing slice of models over time unless it is periodically revised.

stats.label: EU AI Act general application · world’s first comprehensive AI law
stats.note: The rules land in stages: bans from February 2025, general-purpose model duties from August 2025, and the high-risk tiers not until 2027 and 2028.
stats.detail: Entered into force August 1, 2024. Prohibited practices (e.g. social scoring, manipulative systems) applied from February 2, 2025. General-purpose AI model duties, transparency, copyright compliance, and systemic-risk assessment for models trained above 10^25 FLOP, applied from August 2, 2025. From August 2, 2026 the Commission began enforcing the Act’s general rules, including the Article 50 transparency and AI-content labeling duties. The high-risk tiers then moved: the Digital Omnibus, politically agreed in May 2026 and in force since July 27, 2026, deferred stand-alone high-risk systems (biometrics, employment, education, migration) to December 2, 2027 and AI embedded in regulated products (toys, lifts, etc.) to August 2, 2028.
stats.source_label: European Commission, AI Act regulatory framework

stats.label: Documented real-world AI harm reports · AI Incident Database
stats.note: A crowdsourced running tally of real-world AI harms and near-misses since 2020: more than 1,600 logged, none of them mass-casualty or civilization-scale.
stats.detail: Maintained by the Responsible AI Collaborative; entries range from biased hiring and lending algorithms to autonomous-vehicle crashes, deepfake fraud, and chatbot-linked harms. Reporting is voluntary and citizen-submitted rather than a random sample: it likely understates true incidence while overrepresenting cases that made the news. No entry to date documents a mass-casualty or civilization-scale event.

stats.label: Senate vote against a 10-year freeze on state AI laws · US preemption fight, 2025
stats.note: A near-unanimous Senate rejected a decade-long moratorium on state AI regulation in July 2025. The push to preempt state law moved to executive action that December.
stats.detail: House Republicans had attached the moratorium to a 2025 budget reconciliation bill; the Senate stripped it 99-1 in July 2025. Biden’s 2023 AI executive order (EO 14110) had already been revoked by Trump’s EO 14148 in January 2025. In December 2025, Trump’s EO 14365 sought to preempt state AI laws through other means (funding conditions, a Justice Department litigation task force) rather than a legislated moratorium; California (SB 53), Colorado, and dozens of other states continue to legislate independently.
stats.source_label: Regulation of artificial intelligence in the United States

stats.label: Dollar threshold defining a reportable ‘catastrophic’ AI incident · California SB 53
stats.note: Fifty or more deaths or serious injuries counts as catastrophic too, and crossing either line means reporting to the state within 15 days, or immediately if harm is imminent.
stats.detail: Applies to ‘large frontier developers’: annual revenue above $500 million, training models above 10^26 FLOP. Requires a published safety framework describing catastrophic-risk testing, incident reporting to California’s Office of Emergency Services, and protected anonymous whistleblowing channels for employees who reasonably believe the company is substantially endangering public safety. Took effect January 1, 2026, the first US state law written specifically for frontier model developers rather than AI use generally.
stats.source_label: Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53)

stats.label: Training-compute threshold that triggers binding duties · EU vs California

series.label: California SB 53
series.source_label: Cal. SB 53, Transparency in Frontier AI Act

stats.note: Both regimes count floating-point operations (FLOP), the raw arithmetic a training run burns: California set its bar a full order of magnitude above the EU’s, and both use training compute as a proxy for capability rather than capability itself, so the EU rule reaches models ten times smaller.
stats.detail: Neither threshold has been tested against a genuinely novel high-capability, low-compute architecture; both regimes reserve the right to designate additional models by other criteria (EU: Commission designation; California: future rulemaking). Compute is the most legible trigger regulators have found, but it is not risk itself — algorithmic efficiency gains mean a lower-compute model can match a higher-compute one’s performance within roughly a year (see compute-growth figure above).

stats.label: Countries endorsing the first joint frontier-AI risk declaration · Bletchley Declaration, 2023
stats.note: The US, China, the EU and UK signed together at the UK’s inaugural AI Safety Summit, the first time governments jointly named catastrophic and loss-of-control risk from frontier AI.
stats.detail: Signed November 1, 2023 at Bletchley Park; a non-binding statement of shared concern and intent to cooperate on frontier AI safety, not a regulatory instrument. Launched a recurring summit series: Seoul (2024), Paris (2025), and India (New Delhi, February 2026), plus a growing network of national AI safety institutes that run pre-deployment model evaluations.

stats.label: Ratifications needed before the first international AI treaty binds · Council of Europe Framework Convention
stats.note: Opened for signature in September 2024 and signed by the US, UK and EU, it binds nobody until five countries ratify it, three of them Council of Europe members.
stats.detail: Full name: Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law. Signature is not accession: the US signed in September 2024 and has not ratified, and roughly 20 signatories, the EU among them, had signed by mid-2026. The convention enters into force on the first day of the month following three months after the fifth ratification, and no entry-into-force date had been announced as of August 2026. It carries broad exceptions for national security uses and no independent enforcement or verification mechanism, a contrast with the specific, compute-triggered duties in the EU AI Act or California SB 53.
stats.source_label: Council of Europe, first global AI treaty opened for signature

stats.label: Rival lab CEOs who co-signed a one-line AI extinction warning · Statement on AI Risk, 2023
stats.note: OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei signed alongside Turing Award winners Hinton and Bengio and hundreds of researchers.
stats.detail: The full statement, released May 30, 2023 by the Center for AI Safety: ‘Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.’ Deliberately one sentence with no policy prescription, so signatories still disagree sharply on what follows from it: pausing development, mandatory pre-deployment testing, or continued scaling with voluntary safeguards.
stats.source_label: Statement on AI risk of extinction

questions.text: How likely are frontier models to enable catastrophic harms — engineered pathogens, mass cyberattacks, loss of control — and on what timeline?
questions.why: Labs’ own safety evaluations show rising scores on bioweapon uplift and autonomous cyber-offense, but critics call the leap from benchmark to real-world catastrophe speculative, and legislative cycles run years behind model releases.
questions.detail:
The case for near-term risk rests on documented trends, not hypotheticals: successive model generations have posted measurable gains on tasks safety evaluators use as proxies for catastrophic potential, from synthesizing dangerous biological information to autonomously executing multi-step cyberattacks. Safety-focused labs and independent evaluators have flagged specific frontier releases as crossing internal risk thresholds that trigger enhanced safeguards, and loss-of-control concerns have moved from academic papers into formal risk frameworks published by the same companies racing to scale. Proponents argue that even a modest annual probability of a severe incident, compounded across a fast-moving field, justifies acting before certainty arrives, because a regulatory response built only after a catastrophic event is a response too late by definition.

Skeptics counter that eval scores measuring narrow task performance are a poor proxy for real-world catastrophic capability, since deploying a bioweapon or a mass cyberattack requires tacit knowledge, materials access, and operational steps no benchmark captures, and current models still fail at many multi-step real-world tasks outside controlled settings. They note that predictions of imminent catastrophic capability have repeatedly slipped in the past, that no frontier model has yet been linked to a documented mass-casualty or infrastructure-scale event, and that treating speculative tail risk as a near-certainty risks regulating against a threat that may be years or a fundamental capability jump away, while doing little about the harms models are already causing today.

questions.text: Does the risk live in a model’s capabilities themselves, or only in specific deployments and uses?
questions.why: Treat capability as the hazard and the model gets regulated before release; treat use as the hazard and regulation arrives sector by sector, after deployment.
questions.detail:
Those who locate risk in capability point out that a sufficiently capable general-purpose model is dangerous the moment it exists, regardless of its intended use: the same weights that answer a chemistry question can, with the right prompting, walk a novice through a dangerous synthesis, and open-weight release makes downstream use impossible to govern after the fact. This is why frontier-focused proposals target the model itself, with mandatory evaluation and disclosure before deployment, rather than waiting for a harmful application to surface, since by the time a catastrophic use is documented in one sector the same capability is already available everywhere else.

Those who locate risk in deployment argue capability alone causes nothing: a model’s weights sitting on a server harm no one until someone builds a product, hooks it to a hospital record system, a hiring pipeline, or a weapons-relevant workflow, and it is that specific integration, not the underlying model, that determines the actual harm and the actual mitigation. They note that sector regulators already have the domain expertise, legal authority, and case law to evaluate AI-enabled medical devices or credit decisions, and that regulating a general-purpose model as if it were inherently hazardous punishes the tool for uses its developer neither intended nor controls.

questions.text: Who should hold rule-writing authority over general-purpose systems: subnational governments, national ones, or international bodies?
questions.why: Rules written closest to the harm are the most responsive, but a technology that ships identically worldwide invites a patchwork nobody can comply with or enforce.
questions.detail:
Proponents of keeping authority close to home, whether at the state or national level, argue that legislatures accountable to the people actually affected by AI harms move faster and adapt more precisely than any international process ever has: US states have already passed AI laws addressing deepfakes, hiring discrimination, and chatbot safety while federal and international efforts stalled, and national governments retain the enforcement teeth, courts, market access, procurement power, that treaties typically lack. They also warn that ceding rule-writing to a single national or international standard risks locking in whichever government’s political priorities happen to hold the pen, with little recourse for jurisdictions that disagree.

Advocates of higher-level, especially international, authority counter that a model trained once and deployed globally makes subnational or even national patchworks close to unenforceable: a developer can simply route around the strictest jurisdiction, and safety-relevant properties of a frontier model do not respect borders any more than the compute used to train it does. They point to early precedents, extraterritorial reach in major regional laws and coordinated evaluation work between national safety institutes and international summits, as evidence that shared standards and mutual recognition are the only way to avoid both a race to the bottom and dozens of incompatible rulebooks.

questions.text: How much would binding safety rules actually slow capability progress, and would slowing cede a decisive geopolitical lead?
questions.why: Industry and national-security voices say compliance costs hand ground to less-constrained rivals; safety advocates say that link is asserted far more often than it is measured.
questions.detail:
Industry and competitiveness-focused voices point to concrete mechanisms: mandatory pre-deployment testing, disclosure, and red-teaming add months to release timelines and headcount to compliance functions, costs that fall disproportionately on the handful of labs actually at the frontier. They argue that in a field where lead time compounds, since state-of-the-art models unlock the tooling and capital for the next generation, even a modest regulatory drag in one jurisdiction while a geopolitical rival regulates lightly or not at all could shift who sets the terms of the technology’s use for a generation, with security as well as economic stakes.

Skeptics of the tradeoff note that the largest frontier labs already run extensive internal safety testing voluntarily, so codifying much of it into law adds process rather than novel delay, and that the jurisdictions cited as competitive threats face their own capital, chip, and talent constraints regulation does little to change. They also point out the claim is asymmetric in practice: it is invoked against nearly every proposed rule regardless of its actual compliance burden, while historical cases of safety regulation in other high-stakes industries did not produce the ceded leadership their opponents predicted.

questions.text: How should present, documented harms weigh against lower-probability catastrophic ones when setting regulatory priorities?
questions.why: Algorithmic bias, labor displacement, and misinformation are measurable today, while pathogen uplift and loss of control are lower-probability and unproven, and the two camps rarely share a room.
questions.detail:
Those who prioritize documented harm point to a growing record of concrete injuries: discriminatory hiring and lending tools, wrongful arrests from faulty facial recognition, deceptive chatbot behavior harming vulnerable users, and labor displacement already underway, all measurable today with identifiable victims. They argue redirecting regulatory attention and funding toward speculative catastrophic scenarios lets present-day harms compound unaddressed while resources chase a hypothetical, and that a regulatory agenda should follow the evidence it actually has rather than the scenario that generates the most attention.

Those who prioritize catastrophic risk argue that severity, not just probability, should drive priority-setting: a low-probability event with irreversible, civilization-scale consequences can warrant more regulatory attention per unit of expected damage than a high-probability but bounded and correctable one, the same logic used in nuclear safety and pandemic preparedness. They also argue the two priorities are not fully zero-sum in practice, since evaluation infrastructure, transparency mandates, and liability rules built for catastrophic risk oversight tend to catch present-day harms too, so treating this as a forced tradeoff undersells how much of the proposed machinery serves both.

questions.text: Are voluntary commitments and codes of practice enough discipline for frontier developers, or does competition inevitably erode them?
questions.why: Frontier labs have quietly loosened safety pledges as release schedules tightened, which reads either as self-regulation failing under a real race or as normal iteration on untested commitments.
questions.detail:
Proponents of voluntary frameworks argue that codes of practice, drafted with direct participation from the engineers who actually understand frontier model behavior, are more technically current and easier to update than statute, and that reputational stakes, public commitments made under scrutiny from press, researchers, and rival labs watching for hypocrisy, create real discipline without the delay or rigidity of binding law. They point to instances where labs have delayed releases, published model cards, or withheld capabilities citing their own commitments as evidence the system produces real behavior change, and warn that binding rules drafted now would ossify practices around today’s understanding of a fast-moving field.

Critics point to a pattern they say is structural, not incidental: safety testing windows compressed as competitive launches clustered together, several signatories to voluntary pledges shipped capabilities the pledges were meant to gate first, and commitments with no external audit or enforcement mechanism leave labs grading their own homework under exactly the commercial pressure the commitments were meant to resist. They argue voluntary discipline holds only until it costs a lab a product launch relative to a rival, at which point the incentive structure, not any individual lab’s good faith, determines the outcome, which is why documented erosion has tended to track competitive launch windows rather than a change of heart.

questions.text: Can regulators define enforceable, durable triggers — compute thresholds, benchmark evaluations — for systems that improve monthly?
questions.why: Compute thresholds calibrated to today’s frontier get cheaper to cross every year as training efficiency improves, and benchmark triggers age faster still as labs train to pass them.
questions.detail:
Supporters of threshold-based regulation argue a bright line, even an imperfect one, beats no line at all: a compute or spend threshold is objective, auditable from cloud billing and chip supply records without inspecting a lab’s actual model, and can be revised by regulation rather than fresh legislation as the frontier moves, which is roughly how existing compute-based triggers were designed to function. They note thresholds do not need to be permanent to be useful, only durable enough to catch the handful of labs actually operating at the frontier at any given time.

Critics counter that both halves of the proposed trigger degrade on a predictable schedule: algorithmic efficiency gains mean a model trained on a fraction of last year’s compute can match or beat it, so a static threshold drifts from catching the riskiest handful of models to catching an ever-wider band of ordinary ones, or conversely misses a genuinely dangerous small model entirely, while benchmark evaluations get gamed or saturated within a release cycle or two as labs train specifically to pass them. They argue this leaves regulators either constantly rewriting the rule, which undercuts the durability the trigger was meant to provide, or enforcing a rule everyone already knows is stale.

positions.name: Innovation-First Competitor
positions.steelman: Speed is the safety strategy: over-regulate now and the AI race goes to Beijing.
positions.description: American AI leadership was built by engineers moving fast, and that speed is the actual safety guarantee: a Western frontier model in wide use beats an authoritarian one nobody can inspect. The real threat is not an unregulated lab, it is fifty state legislatures each writing their own rulebook: in 2025 every state introduced AI legislation and 38 enacted roughly 100 different measures, a compliance patchwork no startup can survive and no foreign rival has to face. US private AI investment hit $109.1 billion in 2024, nearly twelve times China’s $9.3 billion, proof the model is working. One light federal standard protects consumers while keeping American labs ahead; government’s job is to clear the runway on permitting, chips, and export of the full American AI stack to allies, not to write pre-deployment mandates for systems that improve faster than any agency can rulemake.
positions.detail:
The roots run through Marc Andreessen’s Techno-Optimist Manifesto (2023) and a16z’s Little Tech Agenda, which frames AI as the next industry where “regulatory agencies are being green-lit in real time” to do to builders what they did to crypto: strangle it with process before it can compete. President Trump’s January 2025 executive order repealed the prior administration’s AI directive, and the July 2025 America’s AI Action Plan, shaped by White House AI and crypto czar David Sacks and OSTP director Michael Kratsios, turned that philosophy into more than 90 federal policy actions, many of them deregulatory, fast-tracked permitting for data centers and chip fabs, and a mandate for Commerce and State to sell full-stack American AI export packages to allied nations before rivals fill the gap. The Action Plan also directs agencies to weigh a state’s AI regulatory posture when allocating some federal AI funding, a lever aimed squarely at the patchwork problem.

The position isn’t tactically unified. In mid-2025 Senator Ted Cruz attached a ten-year moratorium on state AI laws to the reconciliation bill, trying to force a single national standard through the budget process. It was stripped by a lopsided Senate vote after even sympathetic Republicans balked at preempting state child-safety and consumer-protection laws with nothing federal to replace them. That defeat didn’t kill the goal, it redirected it: proponents now push for a clean, standalone preemption statute and lean on executive tools (funding conditions, procurement rules) while the state-by-state fight continues in the courts and legislatures.

The strongest evidence proponents cite is the scoreboard itself: the Stanford HAI 2025 AI Index shows US institutions producing 40 notable frontier models to China’s 15, and private AI investment at $109.1 billion against China’s $9.3 billion, a gap they credit directly to a lighter regulatory hand. But the same report is also their warning shot: Chinese model performance on benchmarks like MMLU and HumanEval has closed from a double-digit gap in 2023 to near parity in 2024. The lead is real but not permanent, which is exactly why proponents argue this is the worst possible moment to load frontier labs with compliance costs a state-directed rival doesn’t have to carry.
positions.proponents: David Sacks, Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, Michael Kratsios, Ted Cruz
positions.representative_note: The White House’s July 2025 blueprint: 90-plus deregulatory actions, pressure toward federal preemption of state AI laws, and directives to export the full American AI stack to allied nations before rivals close the gap.

positions.name: Comprehensive Regulator
positions.steelman: One rulebook, tiered by risk: the more a system can do, the more it owes.
positions.description: A single horizontal law exists so that no system, no use case, and no future capability jump falls outside the perimeter by accident: it classifies AI by risk and scales the duties to match. Patching sector by sector leaves seams a general-purpose model can slip through, while one risk-tiered statute closes them in advance and gives builders a single predictable rulebook instead of fifty overlapping ones. The EU’s AI Act already proves the approach works: general-purpose models trained above 10^25 floating-point operations have carried mandatory risk assessment, adversarial testing, and incident-reporting duties since August 2025, backed by fines up to 3 percent of global turnover, or 15 million euros, for general-purpose model providers, and up to 7 percent for the Act’s outright prohibitions. That is a legal floor that holds whether or not the market feels like cooperating, and it is already being copied: South Korea has passed its own horizontal, risk-tiered AI law, and Brazil’s Senate has passed a comparable bill now pending in the Chamber of Deputies.
positions.detail:
The horizontal model was not the first draft. The European Commission’s original 2021 proposal was a product-safety regulation built around discrete high-risk use cases, closer in spirit to the sectoral approach its critics still prefer. The release of ChatGPT in late 2022 forced a rewrite: general-purpose and foundation models did not fit neatly into any single use case, so Parliament’s co-rapporteurs, Brando Benifei and Dragoș Tudorache, pushed through a dedicated chapter covering GPAI providers directly, with extra obligations for models judged to carry systemic risk. Political agreement landed in December 2023 after marathon trilogue negotiations, and the Act entered into force in August 2024 with a staged timeline: prohibited practices first, GPAI duties from August 2025, transparency and content-labeling duties from August 2026, and the high-risk tiers deferred by the 2026 Digital Omnibus to December 2027 for stand-alone systems and August 2028 for AI embedded in regulated products.

The systemic-risk line itself, a training-compute threshold of 10^25 FLOP, was a compromise, not a settled science. Comprehensive regulators mostly concede the threshold is an imperfect proxy for what actually makes a model dangerous, but they defend it as the same trade-off every risk-tiered law makes: a measurable, hard-to-game trigger beats an ungoverned gap while better metrics mature, and the law lets the Commission adjust thresholds and add benchmark-based criteria as evaluation science improves. The stronger empirical case for the horizontal design is what economists call the Brussels effect: because global providers would rather meet one compliance standard than run separate EU and non-EU product lines, AI Act-grade practices tend to propagate into markets the law never touched, the same pattern GDPR set for data privacy two decades ago.

Groups like the Center for AI and Digital Policy, led by Marc Rotenberg, back the horizontal design explicitly because narrower rules have a track record of failing: facial recognition and biometric surveillance went substantially unregulated for years under sector-by-sector approaches before anyone closed the gap. Cognitive scientist Gary Marcus has repeatedly pointed to the AI Act as the regulatory floor the United States still lacks. And the model is spreading on its own evidence rather than argument alone: South Korea’s AI Basic Act, passed in December 2024, and Brazil’s AI bill both adopted comparable risk tiers rather than the narrower, model-only or sector-only alternatives on offer.
positions.proponents: European Commission, MEPs Brando Benifei and Dragoș Tudorache (AI Act co-rapporteurs), Center for AI and Digital Policy (Marc Rotenberg), Gary Marcus, South Korea’s AI Basic Act, Brazil’s AI bill
positions.representative_note: World’s first comprehensive, horizontal AI law: entered into force August 2024, GPAI duties binding from August 2025, fines up to 7% of global turnover for the most serious violations.

positions.name: Frontier Safety Mandater
positions.steelman: Catastrophic capability earns mandatory testing, not a promise the lab grades itself on.
positions.description: Duty of care should scale with capability: the handful of models that can uplift bioweapons design, run autonomous cyberattacks, or slip out of human control are categorically different from ordinary software. That means mandatory pre-deployment testing against catastrophic-risk benchmarks, public disclosure of the safety framework a lab actually used, a legal duty to report dangerous incidents fast, and protection for the engineers who see a problem before the public does. This already exists: California’s SB 53 requires frontier developers to publish safety frameworks, report incidents to the state within 15 days, and shield whistleblowers from retaliation, and New York’s RAISE Act added a 72-hour incident-reporting duty carrying civil penalties of up to $1 million for a first violation and $3 million after, enforceable from January 2027. Voluntary commitments did not get there on their own: it took frontier-lab insiders, several forfeiting unvested equity, publishing an open letter in 2024 before labs took whistleblower protection seriously.
positions.detail:
The clearest ancestor of this position is SB 1047, Scott Wiener’s 2024 California bill that would have required frontier developers above a compute threshold to conduct safety testing and hold a positive safety determination before training a covered model. Governor Newsom vetoed it in September 2024, but the coalition behind it, including Center for AI Safety’s Dan Hendrycks as a technical advisor and Encode as a lead sponsor, rewrote it as SB 53, narrowed to transparency and incident reporting rather than pre-training approval, and Newsom signed that version into law on September 29, 2025. New York’s RAISE Act, signed December 19, 2025, extended the same architecture: written safety protocols, annual review, a 72-hour incident-reporting duty, and whistleblower protections that survive contract waivers. A chapter amendment signed March 27, 2026 (S8828, chapter 96) repealed and replaced the original article, pulling it closer to the California model: it dropped the ban on deploying models that pose an unreasonable risk of critical harm, capped civil penalties at $1 million for a first violation and $3 million after, and routed oversight through a new office in the Department of Financial Services from January 1, 2027, a trade proponents accept as the price of getting a second state onto the same architecture.

The whistleblower plank has its own separate history. In June 2024, a group of current and former OpenAI and Google DeepMind staff, including Daniel Kokotajlo, William Saunders, and Jacob Hilton, published A Right to Warn, describing non-disparagement clauses that discouraged departing employees from raising safety concerns; Yoshua Bengio, Geoffrey Hinton, and Stuart Russell endorsed it publicly. That episode is the position’s central piece of evidence that voluntary internal escalation cannot be trusted on its own: employees inside frontier labs said, on the record, that they did not feel safe raising catastrophic-risk concerns through official channels, which is exactly the gap statutory whistleblower protection is built to close.

Internally, the position debates how far to extend the state-by-state model before it needs a federal or international floor: some proponents, including parts of Anthropic’s own policy team, frame SB 53-style transparency law as a stopgap that only a binding federal standard can properly generalize, while advocacy groups like Encode treat state legislation as the durable mechanism in its own right, since it does not require waiting on a gridlocked Congress. The position also has to answer why testing and disclosure duties, rather than the harder pre-approval gate SB 1047 originally proposed, are the right level of intervention; its answer is that mandatory testing plus enforceable transparency lets regulators, courts, and the public verify a lab’s safety claims without handing any single agency a veto over which models get built.
positions.proponents: Yoshua Bengio, Geoffrey Hinton, Stuart Russell, Dan Hendrycks (Center for AI Safety), Sen. Scott Wiener, Daniel Kokotajlo, Encode
positions.representative_note: Advocacy nonprofit that sponsored both SB 53 and the RAISE Act, the first mandatory frontier-AI testing, disclosure, and whistleblower-protection laws enacted in the US.

positions.name: Sectoral Incrementalist
positions.steelman: Regulate what AI does, not what it is: the sector regulators already have the tools.
positions.description: Harm lives in what an algorithm does inside a hospital, a bank, or a hiring pipeline, not in the parameter count of the model behind it, so the FDA reviewer, the EEOC investigator, and the bank examiner are the right people to police it. One statute for a technology that reshapes itself every few months is obsolete or over-broad before the ink dries, while adapting proven sector-specific rules case by case keeps pace. It is already working: the FDA’s public list of AI-enabled devices runs to many hundreds of authorizations and grows with every update, every one cleared through the existing device framework without Congress passing a single AI-specific law, and the FTC has said plainly that there is no AI exemption to the laws on the books. Give every domain regulator the mandate and expertise to reach AI-enabled harms in its own sector, and the coverage is comprehensive without ever having to define ‘AI’ in a general statute.
positions.detail:
The clearest real-world embodiment of this view is the UK’s 2023 AI white paper, which deliberately rejected both an EU-style horizontal AI act and a new dedicated AI regulator. Instead it directed existing bodies, the ICO, the FCA, the MHRA, Ofcom, the CMA, to apply five cross-sectoral principles within their own remit, on the reasoning that ‘a context-specific approach allows regulators to weigh the risks of using AI against the costs of missing opportunities to do so.’ That is the core bet of this position: a regulator who already knows a sector’s failure modes will spot an AI-shaped version of them faster than a new AI office ever could.

The strongest evidence proponents point to is how far an old framework has already flexed without new legislation. The FDA released its AI/ML-Based Software as a Medical Device Action Plan in 2021, and by December 2024 had finalized guidance on Predetermined Change Control Plans, letting a device’s algorithm keep learning after approval without returning to review each time. The device count that resulted, a public FDA list running to hundreds of authorized AI-enabled devices and lengthening with each update, is offered as proof a decades-old statute can absorb a fast-moving technology. The EEOC’s 2023 guidance applying existing Title VII and ADA analysis to algorithmic hiring tools, and FTC actions like its Rite Aid facial-recognition order brought under standing Section 5 authority, are cited as the same pattern playing out in employment and consumer protection.

The sharpest objection, that a general-purpose model cuts across every sector at once and no single regulator owns the risk of a chatbot helping design a pathogen or run a cyberattack, is one proponents like Thierer and Chilson answer rather than duck: they argue that is a narrow, genuinely novel national-security problem best handled through export controls and existing security agencies, not a reason to impose a compliance regime on every hiring tool and radiology algorithm in the country. Stacking a horizontal AI law on top of sectoral rules that are already reaching real harms, in their telling, mainly slows down the overwhelming majority of AI use that hurts no one.
positions.proponents: Adam Thierer (R Street Institute), Neil Chilson (Abundance Institute, former FTC chief technologist), Daniel Castro (Information Technology and Innovation Foundation), UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (2023 AI white paper)
positions.representative_note: Longtime technology policy scholar who argues existing sectoral law already reaches AI harms and that a dedicated federal AI statute would ossify a fast-moving field.

positions.name: Open-Weights Advocate
positions.steelman: You can’t audit a model you aren’t allowed to have. Openness is the safety mechanism.
positions.description: Every safety claim a closed lab makes is a claim only that lab can check, and open weights invert that: anyone can red-team the model, reproduce the evaluation, publish what broke, and fix it, which is how security has worked in every other part of software. Model-level licensing, pre-deployment approval, and liability for what downstream users do are not neutral safeguards, they are a moat priced so that the three or four companies already at the frontier can clear it and nobody else can. The US government studied exactly this question and did not find the case for closing weights: after 332 public comments, its July 2024 report concluded the evidence was not sufficient to restrict open model weights and recommended monitoring instead, and the 1,821 signatories of the 2023 Joint Statement on AI Safety and Openness, Yann LeCun and Andrew Ng among them, put it more bluntly: openness is an antidote, not a poison. The strategic case has only sharpened since Chinese labs began shipping open weights the world downloads by default, because a closed-only West does not stop open models, it only stops Western ones.
positions.detail:
The policy anchor is NTIA’s report on dual-use foundation models with widely available model weights, ordered by the 2023 AI executive order and published July 30, 2024. It weighed the marginal risk of open weights against closed models and against technology already in circulation, concluded that current evidence is not sufficient to determine either that restrictions are warranted or that they will never be appropriate, and recommended that the government collect evidence, build benchmarks and thresholds, and keep the option of acting later. Open-weight advocates read that as the correct default: monitor, do not license. The same fight runs through the EU AI Act, which exempts free and open-source general-purpose models from parts of its documentation duties but withdraws the exemption the moment a model is designated as carrying systemic risk, and through SB 1047, whose loudest opposition came from developers asking what a lab owes for weights that anyone can download, modify, and fine-tune.

Openness is not one camp. The research wing, EleutherAI, Hugging Face, and academic labs, wants weights released because reproducibility and independent interpretability work are impossible without them, and it is often as critical of the largest AI companies as any safety advocate. The commercial wing releases weights as competitive strategy, and it is the target of the openwashing critique: Meta calls Llama open source while its license limits who may use it, which is why the Open Source Initiative spent 2024 drafting a formal Open Source AI Definition to mark the line. Proponents in the research wing argue the distinction is a policy question, not a branding one: rules should attach to what a release actually lets outsiders verify, not to the word on the license.

The 2025-26 turn moved this from a licensing argument to a strategic one. DeepSeek’s R1 and Alibaba’s Qwen releases put capable open weights into global circulation on permissive terms, and America’s AI Action Plan, otherwise a deregulatory document, carved out a section arguing that open models carry geostrategic value and that the federal government should create a supportive environment for them. Advocates take the hardest objection head on rather than dodging it: once weights are public, safety fine-tuning can be stripped and there is no recall. Most of the camp accepts capability-specific limits at the point where uplift is demonstrated, biological design tools first among them, and argues the honest comparison is not open versus safe, but open versus a handful of firms auditing themselves and publishing the grade.
positions.proponents: Yann LeCun, Andrew Ng, Stella Biderman (EleutherAI), Clément Delangue (Hugging Face), Mozilla, Meta
positions.representative_name: NTIA report on open model weights
positions.representative_note: The US government’s July 2024 review of dual-use models with widely available weights: after 332 public comments it found the evidence insufficient to justify restricting weight release, and recommended active monitoring instead.

positions.name: National Security Realist
positions.steelman: Strategic infrastructure, not a consumer app: govern the chips and the weights.
positions.description: Frontier AI is not a consumer product to be policed like one, it is strategic infrastructure, and the leverage sits where the physical chokepoints are: advanced chips, the fabs and data centers that host them, and the model weights themselves. Those chokepoints are few and reachable with instruments the government already runs, export licensing, security clearances, personnel vetting, counterintelligence, none of which require Congress to define ‘AI’ in a statute first. This is also the approach with an actual track record: the US has restricted advanced AI chip exports to China since October 2022, and a June 2026 executive order pushed the same logic past hardware, directing a framework in which developers work with the government to pick the trusted partners that get early access to designated frontier models. Meanwhile the labs holding some of the most strategically valuable files in the country still secure them like ordinary software companies: RAND’s 2024 review mapped 38 distinct ways to steal a set of model weights and concluded that defending against the most capable state actors will take far more investment than labs make today.
positions.detail:
The position’s two founding texts arrived within a year of each other. Leopold Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness, published June 2024, argued that frontier labs hold strategically decisive material behind startup-grade security, and that a government treating AGI as an ordinary private product would wake up to find the weights already copied. Dan Hendrycks, Eric Schmidt and Alexandr Wang’s Superintelligence Strategy, published March 2025, supplied the strategic frame: Mutual Assured AI Malfunction, or MAIM, the claim that any state’s visible bid for unilateral AI dominance invites preemptive sabotage from rivals, so the stable policy is deterrence paired with nonproliferation of advanced chips and weapons-relevant capabilities, plus domestic competitiveness in chip manufacturing and talent. The US-China Economic and Security Review Commission took the harder line in its 2024 annual report, recommending that Congress ‘establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program dedicated to racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) capability.’

These are the instruments actually in force, which is the camp’s strongest claim on the debate. The US has restricted exports of advanced AI chips to China since October 2022, with the regime tightened, loosened and relitigated repeatedly since: a 15 percent cut of Nvidia’s H20 sales to China in August 2025, 25 percent extended to the H200 in December 2025, a 25 percent semiconductor tariff proclamation in January 2026, and a formalized BIS license review policy the same month. In June 2026 Executive Order 14409, Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security, carried the same logic past hardware without adding an export rule: it directs criteria for designating covered frontier models, a classified process for benchmarking models’ cyber capabilities, a voluntary framework in which developers help the government select trusted partners for early access to those models, and expanded federal programs for AI-enabled cyber defense. On the security plank the camp’s central citation is RAND’s May 2024 study of frontier model weights, which identified 38 meaningfully distinct attack vectors, defined five security levels, and concluded that securing weights against top cyber-capable nation-states will require significantly more investment than frontier labs currently make.

The camp is not united, and its sharpest fights are with the administration executing pieces of its policy. Hardliners read the chip revenue-share arrangements as selling the chokepoint they spent three years building, and legal analysts have argued those arrangements exceed executive authority, since the Export Control Reform Act bars charging for export licenses and the Constitution bars taxes on exports. The MAIM authors reject the Manhattan Project framing the USCC recommended, on their own logic: a visible national crash program is precisely the move that invites sabotage. And the camp has to answer the objection that controls accelerate what they were meant to slow, since restricted rivals build indigenous stacks and route around the rules through smuggling and offshore cloud access. Its answer is enforcement rather than retreat, including the firmware-level chip security and location verification Superintelligence Strategy proposes, on the reasoning that a leaky chokepoint is still a chokepoint and no comparable lever exists anywhere else in the stack.
positions.proponents: Dan Hendrycks (Center for AI Safety), Eric Schmidt, Alexandr Wang, Leopold Aschenbrenner, Sella Nevo (RAND), Center for Security and Emerging Technology, US-China Economic and Security Review Commission
positions.representative_note: Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang’s March 2025 paper: deterrence through Mutual Assured AI Malfunction, nonproliferation of advanced chips and model weights, and domestic competitiveness, in place of a national crash program.

positions.name: Present-Harms Accountability
positions.steelman: Regulate the harms that already have victims, not the ones in the pitch deck.
positions.description: Which risks count as the serious ones is itself a governance decision, and right now it is being made by the companies with the most to gain from the answer. The harms with named victims are already documented: wrongful arrests from face recognition that NIST measured returning false matches for Asian and Black faces 10 to 100 times more often than white ones, opaque denials in housing, credit and benefits, workers managed by systems they cannot contest, data taken without consent. Frontier governance should follow that evidence and bind the companies rather than the abstractions: no self-attestation, no safety framework a lab writes and then grades itself against, conditions on public money and public procurement, and the burden on the developer to show a system is not harmful before it ships. The catastrophic-risk frame asks regulators to look past the concentration of power in front of them toward a hazard only the labs claim to be able to measure, when corporate control of an infrastructure everyone else has to build on is the civilization-scale risk that can actually be verified today.
positions.detail:
The fullest statement of the position is AI Now’s Artificial Power: 2025 Landscape Report (Kate Brennan, Amba Kak and Sarah Myers West, June 2025), which argues that AI is less something the public uses than something used on it, and that the governing question is therefore who holds power over the infrastructure. Its asks are structural rather than model-level: enforce the laws already on the books, attach binding conditions to procurement and public financing, and treat concentration in compute, cloud and data as the object of regulation rather than the backdrop to it. The burden-of-proof plank was set out earlier, in the 2023 Zero Trust AI Governance framework published by AI Now with EPIC and Accountable Tech: at every phase of the lifecycle, the company should have to prove its system is not harmful, rather than the public having to prove it is.

The camp’s sharpest claim is about agenda-setting. Timnit Gebru and Émile Torres argued in First Monday (April 2024) that an undefined artificial general intelligence cannot be tested for safety in the first place, and that the ideology behind the pursuit directs money and attention toward speculative rescue scenarios instead of the systems already deployed on people. Applied to governance, the argument is concrete: several of the labs that signed the 2023 extinction statement spent the following two years lobbying for federal preemption of state AI laws, so treating their framing as the field’s risk agenda is not neutral, it hands them the rulebook they are asking for.

The position is not one program. A civil-liberties wing, EFF and the ACLU among them, is wary of new licensing regimes of any kind and prefers enforcement, liability and disclosure duties that existing courts and agencies can already run, on the theory that permission-based regimes get captured by whoever can afford the paperwork. A structural wing, AI Now and DAIR closest to it, wants merger review, limits on public subsidy, and public alternatives to privately held compute. Both answer the obvious objection, that they are simply betting against catastrophe, the same way: they are not forecasting that nothing goes badly wrong, they are pointing out that every remedy proposed for the speculative case routes authority and legitimacy back through the firms building the systems, and that a regime unable to stop a documented harm today should not be trusted with a hypothetical one tomorrow.
positions.proponents: Timnit Gebru (DAIR), Emily Bender, Meredith Whittaker (Signal), Joy Buolamwini (Algorithmic Justice League), Amba Kak and Sarah Myers West (AI Now Institute)
positions.representative_note: Its Artificial Power: 2025 Landscape Report argues that AI policy has organized itself around the largest labs’ framing, and that binding rules should target corporate power, procurement and public money instead.

positions.name: Global Coordinator
positions.steelman: A risk that stops at no border needs a floor every major power signs and verifies.
positions.description: Frontier AI is trained by a handful of labs and misused across borders no single regulator can reach, so safety has to be negotiated the way nuclear nonproliferation was: a shared floor every major power signs onto and verifies together, not a patchwork each government hopes the others copy. The training compute for the largest models is unusually traceable, concentrated in a few fabs and cloud providers, exactly the kind of chokepoint that made IAEA-style verification enforceable rather than aspirational. This is not hypothetical: 28 countries including the United States and China signed the 2023 Bletchley Declaration, and by 2025 thirty governments were backing the International AI Safety Report, chaired by Yoshua Bengio with 96 contributing experts, the first document of its kind to reach cross-bloc scientific consensus on frontier risk. What is missing is not the will to talk but a standing body with the mandate to keep pace: shared evaluations, a compute-monitoring regime, and rules that update as capabilities do, not one summit communique every eighteen months.
positions.detail:
The push for a global regime traces to the 2023 AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park, the first summit of its kind, which launched an annual cycle now running through Seoul (2024), Paris (2025), New Delhi (2026) and Geneva (2027). Each summit has added infrastructure: an international network of AI Safety Institutes, the Bengio-chaired safety report, and the UN High-Level Advisory Body’s Governing AI for Humanity report, which called for an IPCC-style International Scientific Panel on AI and a standing Global AI Governance Dialogue inside the UN system.

The coalition is not united on how much teeth the regime should have. Some proponents, including UN Secretary-General António Guterres, have called outright for an IAEA-style global watchdog with inspection powers over frontier training runs; others, wary of handing any single body enforcement authority over the technology itself, favor the softer summit-and-shared-evaluation model that already exists and would rather extend it than replace it. There is a parallel argument over what to govern: whether compute thresholds and chip-level verification, the approach Robert Trager and the Oxford Centre for the Governance of AI have detailed, are a workable lever, or whether they mainly hand export-control power to whichever states already dominate chip manufacturing.

The clearest evidence the coordinators point to is that rival geopolitical powers have already coordinated once it mattered: the United States and China both signed Bletchley and both back the International AI Safety Report, something neither trade policy nor cyber norms has achieved at comparable speed. Ian Bremmer and Mustafa Suleyman’s 2023 Foreign Affairs essay The AI Power Paradox, which proposed a hybrid IPCC-IAEA-CERN body for frontier AI, remains the most cited blueprint for what a standing institution could look like.
positions.proponents: Yoshua Bengio, UN Secretary-General António Guterres, Ian Bremmer, Mustafa Suleyman, Robert Trager, UN High-Level Advisory Body on AI
positions.representative_note: Chairs the International AI Safety Report, the first cross-bloc scientific consensus document on frontier AI risk, backed by 30 governments including the United States and China.

positions.name: Pause Advocate
positions.steelman: Alignment isn’t ready and there is no second try: stop scaling until safety is shown.
positions.description: Some risks are too irreversible to run as an experiment on the whole species, and losing control of a smarter-than-human system is the paradigm case: there is no second try. Interpretability and alignment research have not caught up to what frontier labs are already training, so the only proportionate response is to stop scaling until safety is demonstrated, not merely promised. This is not fringe alarmism: in the 2023 survey of 2,778 published AI researchers, between 38 and 51 percent gave at least a 10 percent chance that advanced AI leads to outcomes as bad as human extinction, and Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio now back a halt or hard restrictions on the most capable systems. A voluntary, unilateral pause just hands the lead to whoever cares least about safety, so the actual ask is a binding, verifiable, international moratorium, enforced the way nuclear material is.
positions.detail:
The intellectual roots go back to Nick Bostrom’s Superintelligence (2014) and the Machine Intelligence Research Institute’s decade of work arguing that a sufficiently capable optimizer pursuing the wrong goal is catastrophic by default. The movement went public in March 2023 with the Future of Life Institute’s open letter calling for a six-month pause on training systems more powerful than GPT-4; PauseAI, founded weeks later by Dutch entrepreneur Joep Meindertsma, turned that into standing activism, picketing Microsoft’s Brussels office, the Bletchley Park AI Safety Summit, and the 2024 Seoul Summit across 13 countries. By late 2025 the coalition had widened into the Statement on Superintelligence, calling for a prohibition on developing superintelligence until there is broad scientific consensus it can be done safely and strong public buy-in; it drew over 70,000 signatures, including Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, a breadth pause advocates cite as proof the concern isn’t confined to any one ideological camp.

The camp splits on mechanism. Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares, in their 2025 book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, argue that voluntary or single-country action is close to worthless and that only a treaty-backed international ban, monitored the way nuclear enrichment is monitored and enforced against violators including rogue data centers, is credible; Connor Leahy’s ControlAI campaigns UK and EU legislators toward the same binding-treaty end. Meindertsma’s PauseAI wing puts more weight on protest, public opinion, and incremental compute-threshold rules building toward an IAEA-style body. Both wings reject the idea, popular even among some safety researchers, that continued scaling is needed to make progress on alignment itself: they argue racing to stay ahead on capabilities has never actually been paired with racing to stay ahead on safety, and that labs’ own safety teams keep getting overruled or hollowed out under competitive pressure.

Pause advocates point out that even the labs building frontier models cannot fully explain why a given model produces a given output: interpretability lags capability by a wide and growing margin, so safety claims about systems not yet built rest on extrapolation, not measurement. They also point to precedent that moratoria are not naive: the 1975 Asilomar conference paused recombinant DNA research until safety protocols existed, and the Montreal Protocol phased out CFCs on a binding global timetable despite deep economic interests on the other side. Their reply to the objection that a pause just cedes the lead to less careful actors is that a verified treaty, not a unilateral pause, closes that gap, and that the same objection was raised against nuclear non-proliferation and proved wrong there too.
positions.proponents: Eliezer Yudkowsky, Nate Soares, Connor Leahy, Joep Meindertsma, Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio
positions.representative_note: Their 2025 book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies argues neural-network-based AI cannot be reliably aligned with current methods and calls for global coordination to halt large-scale frontier AI development, verified like nuclear material, until alignment is solved.

crux.lead: Should rules wait for a demonstrated harm, or reach upstream to the training run itself?
crux.lead_highlight: reach upstream to the training run itself?
crux.subtitle: Camps split on two axes: how far upstream of demonstrated harm binding rules should reach, from liability after the fact to a halt on scaling. The second axis is where the rule gets written: a statehouse, a capital, or a treaty.
crux.empirical: Whether frontier models can enable engineered pathogens, mass cyberattacks, or loss of control on timelines law can meet; whether compute and benchmark thresholds keep tracking danger in systems that improve monthly; and whether binding rules measurably slow capability progress, and any slowdown actually cedes a decisive geopolitical lead.
crux.values: The burden of proof: must harm be demonstrated before rules bind, or safety demonstrated before scaling continues? Beneath that sits how present, documented harms should weigh against lower-probability catastrophe, and who legitimately holds the pen over a general-purpose technology: states, nations, or international bodies.
